subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 5 of Year 4 Computing at Ehel Academy. This unit answers two big questions: What does a computer scientist actually do? and How do robots help people at work? Now you meet the real people who do this for a living, and discover that the clever machines around us — from a delivery drone to a robot that helps a doctor — were built by computer scientists.
learningPath: Preview the goals, key words and the tools you will use
Read the concept explainers and study the code examples
Follow the methods and worked examples
Build the activities, debug your work and play the games
Apply, explain and finish the Unit Project and Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Computing 0672 — Stage 4 Teacher & Parent Guide, Activity Sheet and Mini-Project. Teacher-directed prose was rewritten into learner-facing explainers so the unit teaches with no adult present.

outcomes: Say what a computer scientist is — a person who uses computational thinking to work with computer hardware and software.
Name some roles a computer scientist can have (hardware engineer, games developer/programmer, software developer, data analyst, robotics engineer).
Describe what almost all computer scientists do: look at a problem and decide how to solve it, break a big problem into smaller ones, and work in a team.
Give examples of robots in delivery, transport, food and healthcare, and say what each does.
Explain what a sensor is and what a drone is.
Think like a computer scientist by writing a simple algorithm (steps in the right order) for a robot to follow.

concepts.title: What is a computer scientist?
concepts.explanation: A computer scientist is a person who uses computational thinking — solving a problem by breaking it into clear steps — to work with computer hardware and software. They create, design and build things to solve problems: writing the software for an app, helping design a robot to pack boxes in a factory, or building a new computer part. On your way here you passed traffic lights, a car, a phone, the fridge at home. Every one has a computer inside, and a computer scientist helped make it work. A computer scientist is someone who is very good at solving problems with computers — by thinking in steps.
concepts.example: Answer this in your own words, out loud or on paper: What is a computer scientist? Then check your answer against the explanation above.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you understand that computational thinking means breaking a big problem into smaller ones?

concepts.title: So many roles! Meet five computer scientists
concepts.explanation: A computer scientist can have many different roles — you will meet five. Yet in almost every role they do the same three things: look at a problem and decide how to solve it, break a big problem into smaller ones, and work as part of a team — often with people who know little about computing, like artists and shopkeepers. Introduce the five computer scientists one at a time, like a little parade
concepts.example: Find one real example of so many roles! Meet five computer scientists around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you know that computer scientists work in teams, not alone? Can you name at least one of the three things almost all computer scientists do? Can you name two or three different roles a computer scientist can have?

concepts.title: Robots at work: delivery and transport
concepts.explanation: Robots are machines that can be programmed to do tasks, and they help people in many industries. Today, two: delivery and transport. For delivery, some companies use flying robots called drones to carry packages, and some restaurants use small ground robots to bring food. For transport, a driverless vehicle (also called an AV) drives itself using sensors — devices that detect things around it, like other cars and the road edge. There are driverless cars, buses and even trains. When a package arrives, a person usually brings it. But some companies now use a drone — a little flying machine with no pilot on board, controlled from far away — to fly it to you. Others use a small robot on wheels on the pavement. A driverless car has no human driver.
concepts.example: So how does it not crash? It is covered in sensors — devices that sense what is around the car, like eyes and ears made of electronics — and its computer uses them to steer safely.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you understand that a driverless car uses sensors to “see” and does not need a human driver?

concepts.title: Robots at work: food and healthcare
concepts.explanation: Two more industries. In the food service industry, robot waiters can greet customers, take an order, serve food and clear dishes, and some robots even prepare food. In healthcare, robots can help surgeons during operations, robotic limbs (a robotic arm or hand) help injured or disabled people pick up and hold objects, and care robots can check a patient's temperature, bring medicine, and help keep hospitals clean. Imagine a cafe where a friendly robot rolls up, greets you and brings your food — that is a robot in the food service industry. In a hospital, a robot can help a doctor operate very steadily.
concepts.example: A robotic hand can help someone hold a cup again. A care robot can check how a patient is feeling and bring their medicine.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you understand that healthcare robots assist people rather than replace you? Can you name one way a robot helps in food service and one way it helps in healthcare?

concepts.title: Think like a computer scientist: write an algorithm
concepts.explanation: A robot only knows what to do because someone wrote it an algorithm — a set of steps in the right order. Choose a job everyone can picture: a delivery robot taking a package from the shop to a house. Try it: This is the core of the session and is enough on its own. Check yourself: Can you understand that a robot follows its steps exactly, so the order really matters? Can you put the steps of an algorithm in a sensible order?

terms: computer scientist
A person who uses step-by-step thinking to work with computer hardware and software.
hardware
The parts of a computer you can touch.
software
The programs that tell a computer what to do.
computational thinking
Solving a problem by breaking it into clear steps.
algorithm
A set of steps, in the right order, to do a job.
robot
A machine that can be programmed to do tasks.
sensor
A device that detects something around it, like heat, light, sound or movement.
drone
A flying machine with no pilot on board, controlled from far away.
driverless vehicle
A vehicle that drives itself using sensors, with no human driver. Also called an AV.
programmer
A computer scientist who writes programs (code).
data analyst
A computer scientist who collects and organises data to answer questions.
robotics engineer
A computer scientist who designs and builds robots.
